source.title: Braking index of isolated pulsars: open questions and ways forward

accepted.question_text: What physical spin-down model can explain isolated pulsars whose braking index, defined observationally from angular velocity Ω and its first and second time derivatives as n = ΩΩ̈/Ω̇², is measured in the range about 1 < n < 2.8, even though the standard magnetic-dipole-radiation model predicts n = 3 and the canonical particle-wind, magnetic-dipole-radiation, and quadrupole-radiation torque mechanisms predict n = 1, 3, and 5 respectively?
accepted.context_brief: Mismatch between observed and canonical pulsar braking indices

evidence.quote: The MDR model predicts n exactly equal to 3. Selected observations of isolated pulsars provide rather precise values of n, individually accurate to a few percent or better, in the range 1 < n < 2.8, which is consistently less than the predictions of the MDR model. In spite of an extensive investigation of various modiﬁcations of the MDR model, no satisfactory explanation of observation has been found as of yet.
For each mechanism described above, the t heoretical braking index is n = 1, 3, 5 for particle wind, MDR, and quadrupole radiation respectively.
It is clear that none of these observed stars has a bra king index consistent with any of the values produced from theory.

accepted.question_text: For the observed low-frequency isolated pulsars, whose measured spin frequencies are about 1–30 Hz, which physical parameters in the braking torque change with frequency or time enough to move the braking index away from the canonical magnetic-dipole value n = 3, given that changes in moment of inertia below about 160 Hz are too small to reproduce the observed range of braking indices?
accepted.context_brief: Low-frequency torque-parameter evolution versus moment-of-inertia effects

evidence.quote: The frequency dependent solution to the braking index allows for th e problem to be approached from two extreme positions. There can be a dependen ce of frequency where the moment of intertia changes at a rate which brings the bra king index away from the canonical value, or in the limit of very slow rotation, the par ameters governing the torque mechanism can be changing with frequency (or time).

From the ﬁgure it is clear that below this frequency, the change in mo ment of inertia is negligible, and the subsequent deviation from n = 3 is also insigniﬁcant. Noting that the data in Table 1 spans a range of frequencies between abou t 1 - 30 Hz, it is worthwhile to consider changes in the physical parameters of the t orque mechanisms at low frequency.

It is seen that the shape deformation, even for this most deformable star ( i.e. low mass, soft EoS), is small at these frequencies and quite unable to reproduce t he observed range of braking indices.

accepted.question_text: In magnetic-dipole-radiation spin-down of isolated pulsars, where the torque coefficient C is proportional to μ² sin²α, μ is the magnetic moment, and α is the inclination angle between the magnetic moment and the rotation axis, do μ, sin α, magnetic-field structure, plasma outflow, magnetospheric currents, or rotationally driven effects such as phase transitions, density profiles, and superfluidity evolve in a way that lowers the braking index below n = 3 as the pulsar spins down?
accepted.context_brief: Magnetic-field and magnetospheric origins of n < 3

evidence.quote: where µ is the magnetic moment and sin α is the angle of inclination between the magnetic moment and the axis of rotation. It is clear from Eq. 5 that one or both of these values would have to increase as the pulsar spins down to mo ve toward the observed braking index values that are less than n = 3.

The magnetic ﬁeld may increase, decrease, or change alignm ent [20]. The torque may vary with magnetic ﬁeld in a way that is not a pure dipole. Pla sma out- ﬂow may cause currents in the magnetosphere. Interaction with t he magnetosphere in general may play in the torque mechanism [13]. Rotationally driven eﬀ ects such as a phase transition, density proﬁle, and superﬂuidity may also aﬀe ct the magnetic ﬁeld.

Unknown composition and magnetic ﬁeld dynamics play a crucial role in understanding the br aking index, and are important to magnetic dipole radiation and relativistic wind at lo w frequency. These eﬀects are diﬃcult to model as they are not yet well underst ood.

accepted.question_text: How much does a relativistic particle wind contribute to the spin-down of isolated pulsars whose measured braking indices lie between about 1 and 3, given that a pure particle-wind torque has theoretical braking index n = 1, magnetic dipole radiation has n = 3, and the wind torque can depend on the same magnetic-field evolution that affects other torque mechanisms?
accepted.context_brief: Relativistic wind contribution to observed braking indices

evidence.quote: For each mechanism described above, the t heoretical braking index is n = 1, 3, 5 for particle wind, MDR, and quadrupole radiation respectively.

The wind mechanism has a dependence on the magnetic ﬁeld, and thus all of the consideration s explained above can aﬀect the braking index due to the wind. The braking index value f or the wind is n = 1 which is near the lowest measured braking indices shown in Table 1. S ince all values in Table 1 fall between 1, and 3, it is prudent to consider the wind as a possible torque mechanism aﬀecting braking.

accepted.question_text: Can the pulsar braking law be modeled as the polynomial spin-down equation Ω̇ = −s(t)Ω − r(t)Ω³ − g(t)Ω⁵, where s(t), r(t), and g(t) represent wind, magnetic-dipole-radiation, and quadrupole torque mechanisms respectively, so that known low-frequency braking-index measurements can be fitted without detailed knowledge of magnetic-field or composition evolution, the combined wind and magnetic-dipole terms can constrain the magnetic field, and high-frequency extensions can probe mechanisms involving mass, composition, magnetic field, or other neutron-star properties?

evidence.quote: Another approach to this problem considered by Alvarez et. al. [21] is to ex- pand the braking law itself into a polynomial which consists of all assum ed torque mechanisms. In this way, we can assume there are no changes in the magnetic ﬁeld, composition of the star, magnetosphere, etc., and that the pulsa r is rotating at low frequency.

As shown in [21] the braking law can be expanded as, ˙Ω = −s(t)Ω − r(t)Ω3 − g(t)Ω5, (7) where s(t), r(t), and g(t) are functions representing the wind, MDR, and quadrupole torque mechanisms respectively, and Ω is the rotational frequenc y.

Furthermore, the combination of s(t) and r(t) may constrain the magnetic ﬁeld. The polynomial solution may also be expanded into high f requencies which may give insight into other mechanisms at work such as mass, co mposition, magnetic ﬁeld, etc.

accepted.question_text: How can a single cohesive model of isolated-pulsar spin evolution integrate low-frequency torque-mechanism physics, high-frequency moment-of-inertia changes from stellar deformation, physical equations of state, mass dependence, unknown composition, magnetic-field dynamics, and neutron-star core microphysics so that measured braking indices can constrain the poorly known microphysics of rotating neutron stars?
accepted.context_brief: Unified braking-index model and neutron-star microphysics

evidence.quote: The problem of braking index can be approached from two ends. We c an consider very fast rotation where moment of inertia may dominate the spin ev olution, or we can consider very slow rotation where the physics of the braking me chanism must be adjusted to ﬁt the data.

This model can be extended to high frequencies, and to include cons iderations of the unknown values described above. This can also be extended to includ e physical equations of state, and mass dependence.

A single, cohesive investigation of all the above possibilities is necessa ry to our understanding of pulsar spin evolution. The resulting parameters may help to constrain the poorly known micro-physics at work in the cores of rotating neu tron stars.
